paper_metadata.title: A Comparative Analysis of Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks in Binary Credit Defaulting Tasks

summary: A hybrid classical–quantum neural network using a continuous‑variable variational circuit (interferometer–squeezer–displacement–Kerr blocks) was tested for credit‑default prediction on ~17,000 records. The QCNN achieved 97.63% training accuracy (96.21% validation) versus ~91.2% for a classical neural network but required about 70 seconds per training step compared with 7 seconds for the classical model, and was evaluated only on a Strawberry Fields simulator.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for binary credit default prediction using a continuous-variable variational quantum circuit, compared against a classical neural network baseline.

algorithm.variant: Hybrid quantum neural network / QCNN with continuous-variable variational circuit
algorithm.ansatz: Continuous-variable circuit with interferometer, squeezer, displacement, and Kerr gates; repeated for five blocks
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for at least 30 epochs; additional 10 epochs for quantum model

optimizer_settings.learning_rate_schedule: exponentially decayed learning rate for classical model; quantum optimizer settings not otherwise reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Ten LDA-reduced classical features were amplitude-embedded into the quantum circuit using PennyLane/Strawberry Fields; output of prior classical layer encoded into the variational circuit
problem_formulation.objective_function: binary credit default classification minimizing binary cross entropy
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: class imbalance handled by undersampling normal cases to a 3:1 ratio relative to default cases

problem_instance.description: Binary credit default prediction on credit card holder data
problem_instance.dataset_name: Synthetic oversampling for credit card default prediction (Fransiscus Pratikto, 2023)

dataset_specification.description: Over 17,000 credit card holder records; 20 predictor features and one binary target; 10,? actually 20 predictors reduced to 10 by LDA; 10% held out for testing

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Converted Excel to CSV; inspected data types/non-null counts/statistics; dropped null columns and client ID; addressed class imbalance by undersampling normal cases to 3:1; standardized features with StandardScaler; LDA reduced 20 features to 10; one-hot encoded outputs
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Training/validation accuracy and loss tracked over epochs; 10% test split; classical model run for 30 epochs, quantum model for 40 epochs

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; TensorFlow/Keras and scikit-learn for classical preprocessing and baseline model
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Pandas/NumPy data handling; StandardScaler normalization; LDA dimensionality reduction; undersampling for class balance
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Accuracy and loss evaluation on training and validation sets

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: quantum model loss decreased and leveled out after about 15 epochs with higher variability than classical model

speedup_claims.conditions: same dataset and training setup; quantum model trained for 40 epochs vs classical model for 30 epochs
speedup_claims.caveats: No speedup was demonstrated; the quantum model was slower per epoch (70 s vs 7 s) but achieved higher accuracy.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not specified; the paper provides no qubit/mode count, circuit depth, or scaling analysis for the continuous‑variable circuit.
limiting_factors: Experiment executed on a simulator rather than quantum hardware
No complexity analysis or theoretical speedup provided
Small dataset (~17k samples) typical for classical ML benchmarks
Quantum model is significantly slower (≈70 s per step vs 7 s classical)
Quantum resources (modes, parameters, circuit depth) not reported

notes: The paper reports a continuous-variable variational quantum circuit built with PennyLane/Strawberry Fields, but does not specify qubit count, circuit depth, shot count, or gate counts. Hardware is therefore not a named gate-based QPU; it is reported as not_specified rather than inferred to a physical device. The classical neural network is included only as a baseline, not a separate experiment.
The abstract states the QCNN achieved higher prediction accuracy (97.63%) than the classical neural network (91.20%), implying 'quantum advantage'.
However, the experiment is performed on a simulator and the quantum model is ~10× slower per step, with no complexity or scaling analysis, so advantage is not demonstrated under Hoefler criteria.
